He has clear recall, directed behaviour, full awareness throughout and a normal electroencephalogram. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Dissociative amnesia involves an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetting and is not explained by a substance or neurological condition. The fugue subtype adds purposeful travel or wandering with confusion about identity. The diagnostic signature is dissociation between memory systems: autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic knowledge, procedural skills and the ability to form new memories remain fully intact. Organic causes must be excluded, which is what the imaging, toxicology and biochemistry accomplish here. Malingering deserves serious consideration whenever there is an external incentive, but it is not diagnosed merely because an incentive exists, and it requires positive evidence of feigning rather than the coherent selective pattern seen here.
key_points: Autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic and procedural memory remain intact.
Dissociative fugue adds purposeful travel away from home with confusion about identity.
Organic causes including head injury, substances, seizures and thiamine deficiency must be excluded first.
Transient global amnesia spares identity and causes dense anterograde failure with repetitive questioning.
Malingering requires positive evidence of feigning, not merely the presence of an external incentive.
explanation.pearls: Test procedural and semantic memory separately from autobiographical memory in any presentation of amnesia, because preserved ability to drive, read and name the prime minister alongside a lost identity is the pattern of dissociative amnesia, whereas feigned amnesia is usually globally and implausibly dense.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with some combination of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, usually with a history of alcohol dependence or malnutrition, and the amnesia that follows it is anterograde with confabulation. His cranial nerves and gait are normal, his ethanol is zero and he is forming new memories perfectly well. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Loss of autobiographical and identity memory with wholly intact semantic and procedural memory, purposeful travel away from home, and an immediately preceding overwhelming psychological stressor is the defining pattern of this disorder, and organic causes have been excluded. The financial motive raises malingering properly, but a malingerer typically presents with a vague global memory loss rather than this sharply selective sparing of skills, and genuine distress with a personally significant precipitant supports a dissociative process. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Transient global amnesia causes profound anterograde memory failure with repetitive questioning, preserved personal identity and resolution within twenty four hours. He knows the date and can form new memories, and crucially it is his identity that is lost, which transient global amnesia characteristically spares. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: External incentive is present and must be weighed seriously, but malingering is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires positive evidence such as inconsistent performance, dramatic presentation on demand or symptoms that do not follow any known memory architecture. His deficit is neuropsychologically coherent, he is distressed rather than indifferent, and the amnesia itself does nothing to prevent the bankruptcy proceeding. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Non convulsive status causes fluctuating conscious state, impaired attention and automatisms, and it would be detected on electroencephalography. He is fully alert with intact attention and orientation, performing complex purposeful tasks such as driving and using his phone. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Psychogenic non epileptic seizures account for a substantial minority of patients referred to epilepsy services and are typically diagnosed after years of ineffective anticonvulsant treatment. Several features in the recorded event favour a non epileptic mechanism: forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening, side to side head movement, asynchronous limb movements that wax and wane, prolonged duration beyond a few minutes, retained awareness throughout, and the absence of tongue biting, incontinence or injury. A normal postictal lactate also argues against a generalised convulsion. None of these features is individually decisive, which is why video electroencephalography telemetry capturing a habitual event is the diagnostic standard. Diagnosis matters because the treatment is psychological therapy rather than anticonvulsants, and because these patients are otherwise at risk of harmful escalation including intubation for presumed status epilepticus.
key_points: Forced eye closure with resistance to opening is uncommon in epileptic seizures.
Asynchronous waxing and waning movements lasting beyond a few minutes favour a non epileptic mechanism.
Retained awareness with immediate orientation afterwards argues against a generalised convulsion.
Normal interictal electroencephalography occurs in genuine epilepsy and cannot exclude or confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment is psychological therapy, and anticonvulsants should be withdrawn once the diagnosis is secure.
explanation.pearls: Treat failure of three appropriately dosed anticonvulsants as a reason to question the diagnosis rather than to add a fourth, and arrange video telemetry, because these patients are otherwise escalated for years and occasionally intubated for presumed status epilepticus.

options.rationale: Simultaneous video and electroencephalographic recording of a habitual event is the only way to establish whether the behaviour is accompanied by an ictal electrographic discharge, and it is the accepted standard for this diagnosis. Routine interictal studies cannot settle the question because they are frequently normal between genuine seizures as well, so capturing an event is what distinguishes the two. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Adding further anticonvulsants is what happens to these patients for years before diagnosis, exposing them to teratogenic risk, cognitive adverse effects and occasionally intubation for presumed status epilepticus. Failure of three appropriately dosed drugs should prompt a review of the diagnosis rather than a fourth trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A dedicated epilepsy protocol does improve detection of hippocampal sclerosis and focal cortical dysplasia and is worthwhile in drug resistant focal epilepsy. It cannot determine whether these particular events are epileptic, and a structural lesion would not by itself explain semiology this atypical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Prolactin rises after generalised tonic clonic seizures and was formerly used this way, and its sensitivity is poor, it is unhelpful after focal seizures, and it must be drawn within a narrow window against a baseline. A normal result would not exclude epilepsy and so cannot establish the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Loop recorders are used where unexplained transient loss of consciousness may be arrhythmic, typically with abrupt collapse, brief duration and rapid full recovery. Nine minutes of asynchronous movement with retained awareness throughout does not fit a cardiac mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed substantially later than men, frequently after years of treatment for anxiety, depression or an eating disorder, because camouflaging conceals the social communication differences that diagnostic criteria were originally written to capture in boys. Camouflaging means consciously masking difficulty through rehearsed scripts, imitated expressions and prepared conversational material, and it is effortful in a way that produces characteristic exhaustion after social contact rather than anticipatory fear before it. That distinction separates camouflaging from social anxiety disorder, where the fear is of negative evaluation and precedes the encounter. The restricted and repetitive domain is present here as insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and a circumscribed intense interest. Recognition matters because it redirects care from repeated medication trials towards environmental adjustment, sensory accommodation and appropriate support.
key_points: Camouflaging masks social communication difference and is markedly more common in autistic women.
Exhaustion after social effort distinguishes camouflaging from the anticipatory fear of social anxiety disorder.
The restricted and repetitive domain includes insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and circumscribed interests.
Autistic special interests are pleasurable and ego syntonic, unlike the distressing compulsions of obsessive compulsive disorder.
Repeated failure of adequate medication trials should prompt review of the formulation rather than further augmentation.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the fear comes before the social event or the exhaustion comes after it, because anticipatory fear of judgement points to social anxiety disorder while post social depletion from effortful masking points to undiagnosed autism, and the distinction redirects care away from a fourth antidepressant trial.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition
Autism CRC: National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.rationale: Social anxiety disorder is driven by fear of negative evaluation and humiliation, and she explicitly denies fear of judgement, describing instead the effort of appearing natural. Three adequate medication trials without benefit is itself evidence that the original formulation was wrong rather than that more medication is needed. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Compulsions in obsessive compulsive disorder are performed to neutralise a specific feared outcome and are experienced as unwanted and ego dystonic, whereas her counting and her textile interest are neither distressing nor aimed at preventing anything. The examination explicitly notes no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Rehearsing scripts, maintaining topic lists and consciously imitating the expressions of others is camouflaging, an effortful compensation that masks social communication difficulty and is far commoner in women, which is why they are diagnosed later and more often misdiagnosed with anxiety. The exhaustion following social effort rather than preceding it, alongside insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity to clothing labels and a circumscribed intense interest, completes the diagnostic picture. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and little desire for social contact, so the person makes no effort to fit in. She works hard to appear natural and finds it costly, which indicates that she wants social connection and lacks the intuitive means rather than lacking the desire. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.rationale: Chronic depression would involve pervasive low mood with anhedonia over at least two years, and her mood is euthymic on examination and she retains intense pleasure in her special interest. Her fatigue follows social effort specifically rather than being present regardless of activity. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is far more often missed, partly because screening and public awareness both centre on low mood. It commonly presents as repeated presentations about the infant, compulsive checking of breathing, inability to sleep when the baby sleeps, and unwanted intrusive images of harm befalling the baby. Those intrusive images are egodystonic, meaning the mother finds them horrifying and alien, which distinguishes them from the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis and means they do not indicate risk to the infant. Examining the subscale structure of the Edinburgh scale rather than the total score alone is what reveals the anxiety pattern here, with item 10 confirming absence of self-harm thoughts. Treatment is psychological, with cognitive behavioural therapy first line and medication reserved for more severe or non responsive presentations.
key_points: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is more frequently missed.
Items 3, 4 and 5 of the Edinburgh scale form an anxiety subscale that can drive an elevated total score.
Item 10 specifically screens for thoughts of self-harm and must always be reviewed individually.
Egodystonic intrusive images of harm are distressing to the mother and do not indicate risk to the infant.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with medication reserved for severe or non responsive illness.
explanation.pearls: Ask a mother with intrusive thoughts of harm whether the thought is horrifying to her or feels reasonable, because egodystonic unwanted images indicate an anxiety disorder that responds to therapy while egosyntonic beliefs about the baby suggest psychosis requiring urgent admission.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and frequently presents as repeated health seeking for the infant, excessive checking and unwanted intrusive images of harm coming to the baby, in a woman whose mood is preserved. Her Edinburgh score of 11 driven by the three anxiety items with a normal mood and preserved enjoyment fits an anxiety disorder rather than a depressive one, and the intrusive images are egodystonic and therefore not a risk to the baby. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Her total score is above the usual referral threshold, which makes this worth considering, and the diagnosis requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, and she reports preserved mood, preserved enjoyment of the baby and preserved social engagement. The elevated score comes specifically from the anxiety items rather than the depressive ones. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency presenting within days to weeks with delusions, hallucinations, confusion and rapidly fluctuating mood, and it requires urgent admission. Her beliefs are not held with conviction, she recognises the images as unwanted products of her own mind, and there are no psychotic phenomena. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: This involves deliberate falsification or induction of illness in the child to obtain attention through the sick role, and the presenting adult is typically calm and comfortable in medical settings. She is genuinely distressed, is seeking reassurance rather than investigation, and the baby has no fabricated findings. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Some vigilance and worry is entirely normal in new parents, and this has crossed into disorder because it is producing insomnia when the baby sleeps, five medical presentations in three weeks and marked distress. Normalising it would leave a treatable condition untreated and reinforce the reassurance seeking. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics differ from each other in how quickly they reach therapeutic plasma concentrations, and the oral cover required at initiation follows the individual preparation rather than any general rule. Aripiprazole given monthly requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole after the first injection. The risperidone injection requires about three weeks of oral cover because it releases almost no drug for the first weeks. Paliperidone palmitate requires none at all, because the regimen uses a loading dose on day one and a second dose on day eight to reach therapeutic levels directly. Getting this wrong produces a relapse a few weeks after a change that was made specifically to prevent one.
key_points: Oral cover at initiation is determined by the individual preparation, not by depots as a class.
Monthly aripiprazole requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole.
The risperidone long-acting injection requires about three weeks of oral cover.
Paliperidone palmitate requires no oral cover because of its day one and day eight loading.
Long-acting injections reduce relapse driven by missed doses.
explanation.pearls: Write the stop date for the tablets on the prescription and in the clinic letter when you give the first injection, because the relapse that follows a depot change almost always happens in the first month and almost always traces back to the tablets being stopped on the day of the injection.

options.rationale: Halving the dose during the period of lowest injectable concentration is the worst of both options, giving inadequate cover for a fortnight while still requiring tablets. The oral dose is maintained in full and then stopped, not tapered. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

Three weeks of oral cover is exactly right for the risperidone long-acting injection, which releases nothing for about three weeks after administration. Applying that interval here gives a week of unnecessary double treatment and shows the cover period belongs to the preparation rather than to depots as a class. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

One long-acting preparation is designed to be started without oral cover by giving two loading injections a week apart, which is why this belief is common on the wards. That approach belongs to the paliperidone preparation and cannot be transferred to an agent that reaches therapeutic levels slowly. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

This preparation takes several weeks to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations after a single injection, so fourteen days of continued oral treatment covers the gap and is built into the product information. Stopping earlier leaves him subtherapeutic during the very period the change was made to protect. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

Long-acting injections maintain plasma concentrations at least as well as oral treatment and reduce relapse driven by missed doses, which is the problem he has had twice. Permanent dual treatment doubles his exposure and defeats the purpose of the change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Combining a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor can cause severe serotonin toxicity, with hyperthermia, rigidity, clonus and autonomic instability, which is why a complete washout is required rather than a cross taper. The length of the washout is set by the elimination of the drug and any active metabolites. Fluoxetine is the outlier among the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors because its metabolite has a half life of one to two weeks, so five weeks are needed after the last dose, against two weeks for the other agents in the class. Going the other way, two weeks are required after stopping an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor before a serotonergic drug is introduced, because new enzyme must be synthesised. Dose reduction does not substitute for time, since half life is unchanged by dose.
key_points: Serotonin toxicity presents with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia and autonomic instability.
A cross taper is never used between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor.
Fluoxetine requires a five week washout because of its long-acting metabolite.
Other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors require two weeks.
Two weeks are needed after stopping the inhibitor before any serotonergic drug is started.
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine is the one antidepressant where the washout is measured in weeks rather than days, so before any switch involving it, check whether the incoming drug is serotonergic and count five weeks from the last tablet, not from the last clinic visit.

options.rationale: Bridging through a shorter acting agent sounds appealing and would shorten the final washout on paper. It requires the fluoxetine metabolite to be gone before the sertraline is stopped, which it will not be, so the total wait is no shorter and the patient takes an extra medicine for no reason. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

Cross tapering is standard practice between most antidepressants and avoids both discontinuation symptoms and a treatment gap. It is specifically contraindicated with this class, because any overlap between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor risks life threatening serotonin toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

Fluoxetine and its active metabolite have half lives measured in days to weeks, so serotonergic activity persists long after the last tablet and a standard two week gap is not enough. Five weeks allows near complete elimination before an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor is introduced, which is what prevents a severe serotonin toxicity reaction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Two weeks is the correct interval after sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram or paroxetine, whose elimination is complete in that time. Applying it to fluoxetine ignores the metabolite that continues to inhibit serotonin reuptake for weeks afterwards. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Reducing the dose shortens neither the half life nor the elimination time of the active metabolite, so the overlap risk is unchanged. A low starting dose of the new agent does not protect against a reaction that is driven by the combination rather than the dose. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Agomelatine is an antidepressant acting at melatonergic receptors with additional serotonin antagonism, and it is chosen partly because it is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain. Its distinguishing safety issue is hepatotoxicity, ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to rare hepatic failure, and this drives a mandatory monitoring schedule. Liver function is checked before the first dose and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks, and after any dose increase. Treatment is not started if transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and it is ceased if they reach that threshold during treatment or if the patient develops jaundice, dark urine or right upper quadrant pain. Regular alcohol intake and other hepatotoxic drugs increase the risk and are worth quantifying before prescribing.
key_points: Hepatotoxicity is the distinguishing safety concern with this drug.
Liver function is checked at baseline and at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks.
Transaminases above three times the upper limit of normal preclude starting or continuing.
It is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain, which is why patients request it.
Hyponatraemia monitoring belongs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine, not here.
explanation.pearls: Order the baseline liver function test before writing the script rather than with it, because the drug should not be started at all when transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and a result that arrives after the first week has already missed that decision.

options.rationale: Early review at two weeks is appropriate for any newly started antidepressant and should happen here as well. It is not sufficient on its own for this drug, because hepatic injury is usually asymptomatic until it is advanced and is detected only by scheduled blood tests. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

This drug causes dose related transaminase rises and rare cases of hepatic failure, so a baseline is taken before the first tablet and the schedule of repeats covers the period in which injury appears. Treatment is not started when transaminases are above three times the upper limit of normal, and it is stopped if they rise to that level on treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Weekly haematological monitoring of that intensity belongs to clozapine, where agranulocytosis risk is concentrated in the first months. No antidepressant requires this schedule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

Sodium monitoring in the early weeks belongs with the serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine in older patients, where hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is the recognised early risk. It is not the monitoring requirement that distinguishes this drug. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Baseline and follow up electrocardiography is the requirement for citalopram at higher doses and for antipsychotics that prolong the QT interval. This agent has no meaningful effect on cardiac conduction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Clozapine monitoring exists because of agranulocytosis, and the thresholds that trigger cessation are derived from neutrophil reference ranges based largely on European populations. A substantial proportion of people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry have a constitutionally lower circulating neutrophil count, caused by a normal variant affecting neutrophil margination rather than by any defect in production or in immune function. Recognising this matters because otherwise these patients are excluded from the only effective treatment for treatment resistant schizophrenia on the basis of a count that has never been abnormal for them. The evidence for the constitutional pattern here is that the low counts long predate the clozapine, that the lymphocyte count is normal, and that there is no history of recurrent infection. Haematology confirmation allows modified thresholds to be registered with the monitoring service, and monitoring continues rather than stopping.
key_points: Clozapine neutropenia thresholds derive from reference ranges based on European populations.
A constitutional low neutrophil count is common in people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry.
Counts that predate the drug, with normal lymphocytes and no infections, suggest the variant.
Haematology confirmation permits modified monitoring thresholds to be registered.
Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so dose reduction does not help.
explanation.pearls: Look for a full blood count taken years before clozapine was ever prescribed, because a neutrophil count of 1.6 in an admission four years earlier is the single piece of evidence that converts a mandatory permanent cessation into a registered modified threshold.

options.rationale: Immediate cessation with a permanent bar is the correct response to a genuine red result, and it exists because agranulocytosis can progress rapidly to fatal sepsis. Applying it to a count that has always been at this level in this patient discards an effective treatment for treatment resistant illness on the basis of a reference range derived from a different population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

Lithium does raise the neutrophil count by demargination and has been used deliberately for this purpose in specialist settings. Using it to mask a count without first establishing why the count is low removes the very signal that monitoring depends on, and it is not an appropriate first response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

A neutrophil count that sat at the lower limit for years before clozapine was ever started, with a normal lymphocyte count and no infections, describes a benign constitutional variant rather than drug induced marrow suppression. Haematology confirmation allows the monitoring service to register modified thresholds so that a patient who has responded to clozapine is not permanently deprived of it for a count that has never been abnormal for him. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so halving the dose does not reduce the haematological risk while it does risk losing the response that has taken seven months to achieve. Dose reduction is not part of the response to an abnormal count. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine)

Carrying on without action ignores a result that has fallen below the threshold at which the monitoring service requires a response, and it leaves the clinician with no documented basis for the decision. Increased monitoring frequency is part of the management even when a constitutional cause is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is cleared almost entirely by the kidney, so anything that reduces renal clearance raises the concentration quickly. Non-steroidal anti inflammatories are the commonest culprit because patients buy them without mentioning it, and they can raise lithium concentrations by up to half within a week. The early features of toxicity are gastrointestinal upset, a coarsening of the usual fine tremor and unsteadiness, progressing to confusion, myoclonus, seizures and renal failure if unrecognised. The immediate response is to remove the interacting drug and measure the concentration alongside electrolytes and creatinine, since dehydration and renal impairment compound the effect. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazide diuretics interact by the same renal mechanism and deserve the same caution.
key_points: Lithium is renally cleared, so anything reducing renal clearance raises the concentration.
Anti inflammatories can raise lithium concentrations by up to fifty per cent within days.
Early toxicity presents as nausea, coarse tremor and ataxia before confusion appears.
Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors interact by the same mechanism and are no safer.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, receptor blockers and thiazides share the interaction.
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient on lithium what they buy at the supermarket, because ibuprofen and naproxen need no prescription, are not on the medication list you are reading, and are the commonest single cause of a lithium level that has climbed without any dose being changed.

options.rationale: Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors act on the same renal prostaglandin pathway and raise lithium concentrations in the same way, so the substitution offers no protection. Paracetamol is the safe analgesic in this situation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

Dialysis is the treatment for severe toxicity, indicated by reduced consciousness, seizures, myoclonus or renal failure, or by very high concentrations. She is alert, oriented and haemodynamically well, so the level is needed before that pathway is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Lithium toxicity)

Routine three monthly monitoring is appropriate for a stable patient with no new symptoms and no interacting drugs. Deferring here allows a rising concentration to continue toward the confusion, myoclonus and seizures of severe toxicity in a woman already showing neurological signs. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

Non-steroidal anti inflammatories reduce renal prostaglandin mediated blood flow and increase proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium, raising concentrations by up to half within days, and her tremor, nausea and unsteadiness are the early features of toxicity. Removing the interacting drug and measuring the level together establish both the cause and the severity before any dose decision is made. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

Adjusting the lithium around an interacting drug that will be stopped in days creates a moving target and risks subtherapeutic concentrations and relapse once the anti inflammatory is finished. The interacting drug is the one to remove. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision specific and is assessed against four elements: whether the person can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough to decide, weigh it in arriving at a choice, and communicate that choice. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself affect any of these, and the assessment must be made about this decision at this time rather than about the person in general. This man demonstrates all four elements and gives a reason for his refusal that is frightening but entirely rational in origin, so his refusal is valid even though the team considers it unwise. Mental health legislation cannot be used to authorise treatment of a physical condition unrelated to the mental illness. The useful clinical response is to address the specific fear, which is the anaesthetic rather than the surgery, ideally by having the anaesthetist discuss his brother's death with him directly.
key_points: Capacity requires understanding, retention, weighing and communication of a choice.
Capacity is specific to the decision and the moment, not to the person or the diagnosis.
An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness, not unrelated surgery.
Guardianship or the emergency doctrine applies when a person genuinely lacks capacity.
explanation.pearls: When a team says a patient lacks capacity because of a psychiatric diagnosis, ask which of the four elements is missing, because in most of these referrals the answer is none of them and the real problem is a specific fear that nobody has asked about.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.rationale: Sedating a person in order to remove their objection is a deliberate circumvention of a valid refusal and constitutes assault. Analgesia is given for pain on its own merits and never as a route around consent. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.rationale: He understands the information, retains it, weighs it against a reason that is comprehensible and communicates a consistent choice, which is all that capacity requires. A diagnosis of schizophrenia does not remove capacity, and an unwise decision made for a reason a frightened person might genuinely hold is not evidence of incapacity. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.rationale: Substitute decision making is engaged when a person genuinely lacks capacity, and it is the correct pathway for non-urgent treatment in that situation. Seeking it for a person who has capacity overrides a valid refusal through an administrative route and is not lawful. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.rationale: Treating an illness that is currently in remission will not change a decision that is not being driven by psychotic symptoms, and forty eight hours in an inflamed appendix carries a real risk of perforation. Reassessment is appropriate when capacity fluctuates, which is not what is happening here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness itself, not unrelated surgical conditions, so it provides no lawful basis for an appendicectomy whatever the risk. Surgical treatment of a person who lacks capacity proceeds through guardianship arrangements or the emergency doctrine instead. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is inactive as given and relies on cytochrome P450 2D6 to produce endoxifen, the metabolite that provides most of its antioestrogen activity. Antidepressants that strongly inhibit this enzyme therefore reduce the concentration of the active metabolite, and observational data have linked paroxetine in particular with increased breast cancer mortality in women taking tamoxifen. Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are all strong inhibitors and are avoided, while sertraline is moderate and citalopram, escitalopram and venlafaxine have minimal effect. Venlafaxine is preferred in this setting because it combines negligible interaction with useful efficacy against vasomotor symptoms, which are common on tamoxifen and are a major cause of sleep disruption. The same interaction applies to other medicines requiring this enzyme for activation, including codeine and tramadol.
key_points: Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen.
Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are strong inhibitors of this enzyme and are avoided.
Venlafaxine, citalopram and escitalopram have minimal effect on the pathway.
Venlafaxine additionally reduces vasomotor symptoms.
Codeine and tramadol also require this enzyme for conversion to their active forms.
explanation.pearls: Check for tamoxifen before writing any antidepressant for a woman treated for breast cancer, because paroxetine is otherwise a sensible choice for hot flushes and it is the single worst option in this one situation.

options.rationale: Fluoxetine is a potent inhibitor of the same enzyme and carries the same concern about reduced tamoxifen activation. Its long half life also makes any later switch slower and more complicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen effect, so an antidepressant that strongly inhibits that enzyme reduces its efficacy. Venlafaxine has minimal effect on this pathway and has the additional advantage of reducing hot flushes, which is the symptom troubling her most at night. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Paroxetine does reduce hot flushes and is an effective antidepressant, which is exactly why it is prescribed in this situation by mistake. It is the strongest cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality when combined with tamoxifen. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Bupropion has a favourable adverse effect profile in some respects but is also a strong inhibitor of the enzyme in question, so it shares the same problem. It is registered in Australia only for smoking cessation rather than for depression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

Sertraline is a reasonable first line antidepressant generally and is only a moderate inhibitor of this enzyme, so it is safer than paroxetine or fluoxetine here. It still carries more interaction risk than the preferred agent and lacks the vasomotor benefit she specifically needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

explanation.summary: Behavioural symptoms in dementia are usually a response to something rather than a random feature of the illness, and the first step is always to look for the pattern. Aggression confined to one care task, at one time of day, with particular staff, points to that task as the trigger, and in this man the painful shoulder explains why being washed and dressed provokes him when nothing else does. Untreated pain is one of the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia, and scheduled analgesia reduces it substantially in randomised trials, whereas as required dosing depends on a man with dementia asking for it. Antipsychotics in this population increase the risk of stroke and death and are reserved for persistent symptoms causing real risk after non drug measures have been tried. Delirium must always be considered, but it fluctuates, impairs attention and usually has an identifiable precipitant, none of which is present here.
key_points: Behavioural symptoms are usually triggered, so identify the pattern before prescribing.
Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia.
Scheduled analgesia works where as required dosing fails in a person who cannot ask.
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and follow failed non drug measures.
Delirium fluctuates and impairs attention, which distinguishes it from this stable pattern.
explanation.pearls: Read the incident times and the names of the staff involved before you prescribe anything, because aggression clustered around one task at one time of day is a pain or a care approach problem, and regular paracetamol fixes more of these than any antipsychotic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

options.rationale: Aggression confined to one task, at one time of day, with the same staff, in a man who grimaces on shoulder movement, is a response to pain rather than a symptom requiring an antipsychotic. Regular rather than as required analgesia and a modified approach to showering address the actual trigger, and trials show scheduled analgesia reduces agitation in dementia substantially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, worsen confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation in older people with dementia, and their role is confined to brief use in severe distress. Sedating a man before a painful procedure treats the staff's difficulty rather than his pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors have a modest effect on some behavioural symptoms over months and he is already at the maximum usual dose of 10 mg daily. Neither the timeframe nor the mechanism addresses aggression that occurs only during a painful task. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic registered in Australia for this indication and has a place for persistent aggression or psychosis that poses real risk after non drug measures have failed. Starting it first exposes him to an increased risk of stroke and death for a problem with an identified and treatable trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: New agitation in an older person does warrant a search for delirium and infection is a common cause, so the instinct is sound. His attention is preserved, the pattern is stable across weeks rather than fluctuating, he is afebrile and the urinalysis was negative, so this does not fit delirium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Delirium)

explanation.summary: Acamprosate and naltrexone are the two first line relapse prevention medicines in alcohol dependence, and choosing between them usually comes down to organ function and the treatment goal. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, while acamprosate is excreted unchanged by the kidney and is contraindicated instead in severe renal impairment. This man has cirrhosis with a raised bilirubin, low albumin and prolonged clotting, all indicating impaired synthetic function, so acamprosate is the appropriate choice and his normal creatinine confirms it is safe. Disulfiram is avoided because it is itself hepatotoxic. Concurrent opioid use is the other decisive factor, because naltrexone will precipitate withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks analgesia if they are needed later.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally excreted unchanged and is not metabolised by the liver.
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure.
Severe renal impairment is the contraindication to acamprosate.
Disulfiram is hepatotoxic and unsuitable in established liver disease.
Naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks later analgesia.
explanation.pearls: Let the failing organ choose the drug: acamprosate for the damaged liver, naltrexone for the damaged kidney, and neither before you have asked whether the patient is taking any opioid, prescribed or otherwise.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

options.rationale: Disulfiram works only with supervised administration and a clear abstinence goal, both of which he has, so it is not an unreasonable thought. It is hepatotoxic in its own right and has caused fulminant hepatic failure, which makes it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

options.rationale: Psychosocial treatment is the foundation of care and he is already linked with a service, so this is half of the right answer. Pharmacotherapy adds meaningful benefit on top of counselling and withholding it in a man with cirrhosis, for whom any further drinking is dangerous, is the wrong place to be conservative. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

Naltrexone has at least equivalent evidence in alcohol dependence and would be a reasonable first choice in a man with a healthy liver. It undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, and his bilirubin, albumin and clotting all indicate significant synthetic dysfunction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

Acamprosate is eliminated unchanged by the kidney and is not metabolised by the liver, so it is the option that remains available when hepatic function is impaired, and his creatinine is normal. Dosing is by body weight and the contraindication to watch for is severe renal impairment rather than liver disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

Baclofen is renally cleared and has been studied specifically in people with liver disease, which makes it a genuine second line option in this population. The evidence for it remains weaker than for the preferred agent and it carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own, so it follows rather than leads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine binds opioid receptors with higher affinity than heroin or morphine but activates them only partially, so administering it while a full agonist is still bound displaces that agonist and drops receptor activation sharply. The result is precipitated withdrawal, which comes on within an hour, is more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and often destroys a person's willingness to try treatment again. The safeguard is timing rather than dose: the first dose is given only once objective withdrawal signs are present, typically six to twelve hours after short-acting opioids and considerably longer after methadone. Objective signs such as dilated pupils, piloerection, sweating and rhinorrhoea are what count, since subjective craving and anxiety appear far earlier. This man used two hours ago, has pinpoint pupils and no objective signs, so dosing now would reliably produce the reaction.
key_points: Buprenorphine has higher receptor affinity than full agonists but only partial activity.
Dosing while a full agonist is bound displaces it and precipitates withdrawal.
Wait for objective signs, typically six to twelve hours after short-acting opioids.
Longer intervals are needed after methadone or other long-acting opioids.
Reducing the dose does not prevent the reaction, since displacement drives it.
explanation.pearls: Look at the pupils before the first dose, because a patient reporting that he feels terrible with 2 mm pupils and dry skin is anxious rather than in withdrawal, and dosing him then produces the one experience most likely to stop him ever coming back.

sources.label: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.rationale: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with very high receptor affinity, so giving it while receptors are still occupied by a full agonist displaces that agonist and causes an abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Waiting until objective signs such as dilated pupils, gooseflesh, sweating and rhinorrhoea are present confirms the receptors are free enough for the first dose to relieve symptoms rather than provoke them. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.rationale: Methadone is a full agonist and does not precipitate withdrawal, so it can be started without waiting, which makes it a legitimate alternative for someone who cannot tolerate the wait. It carries a substantially higher overdose risk during induction because of accumulation over the first days, so it is a considered choice rather than the default when timing is the only obstacle. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.rationale: Naltrexone is an antagonist used after complete detoxification and requires a full opioid free interval beforehand, so it cannot be started today either. Relapse after antagonist treatment also carries a high mortality because tolerance has been lost. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Opioid dependence)

Symptomatic medicines take the edge off ordinary withdrawal and have a role alongside induction. They do not prevent or adequately treat precipitated withdrawal, which is far more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and frequently ends a person's engagement with treatment altogether. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.rationale: Dose reduction is used to make an induction gentler once the timing is right and withdrawal has begun. It does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, because the reaction is driven by displacement of the full agonist rather than by the size of the dose. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

explanation.summary: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia and carries a set of hazards that require structured monitoring, including neutropenia, myocarditis in the first weeks, constipation progressing to ileus, seizures and cardiometabolic effects. A less well known but clinically critical hazard is the rapid loss of tolerance to its cardiovascular and sedative effects during a break in treatment. When more than 48 hours of doses are missed, the patient must be retitrated from the starting dose rather than resuming their previous maintenance dose, because reinstating the full dose has caused profound hypotension, respiratory depression, seizures and death. Breaks in treatment are common during physical illness, hospital admission and disruption to supply, so the question of how many doses were missed should be asked routinely whenever a patient on clozapine presents.
key_points: Tolerance to clozapine's cardiovascular effects is lost after more than 48 hours
A break of more than two days requires retitration from the starting dose
Retitration after a break can usually proceed faster than initial titration
Physical illness and admission are common causes of unplanned breaks
Ask specifically how many doses were missed at every presentation
explanation.pearls: The 48 hour rule is the one clozapine number that changes management at the bedside: beyond that gap the maintenance dose becomes unsafe and titration restarts at 12.5 mg regardless of how long the patient has been stable.

options.rationale: Continuing at the full dose after tolerance has been lost is the exact scenario that has caused deaths from cardiovascular collapse and seizures. Monitoring does not mitigate a dose the patient can no longer tolerate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Tolerance to the cardiovascular effects of clozapine is lost after more than 48 hours without a dose, so resuming the previous dose risks severe hypotension, sedation and seizures. Retitration from the starting dose rebuilds tolerance safely, and it can usually be done faster than an initial titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Any dose substantially above the starting dose carries the same tolerance related risk, and halving is an arbitrary compromise rather than a recognised approach. The safe restart point is the initial titration dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Abandoning an agent that has given six years of remission in treatment resistant illness would very likely lead to relapse. A missed dose interval is a titration problem, not a reason to change drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Treating the symptom leaves the underlying dosing hazard in place and adds a drug with its own risks. The hypotension is a signal that the dose is no longer tolerated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial agonist at the mu opioid receptor, and this pharmacology explains both its safety advantages and its main induction hazard. Because it binds more avidly than most full agonists, giving it while the receptor remains substantially occupied displaces the full agonist and replaces a high level of activation with a lower one, producing abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Induction is therefore timed by objective withdrawal features rather than by the interval since last use, using a structured scale, and the required wait is longer after long-acting preparations such as slow release morphine or methadone than after short-acting opioids. Subjective distress alone is not adequate evidence of readiness, since anxiety and drug seeking can be present well before the receptor is free. Once established, buprenorphine carries a lower overdose risk than methadone because of its ceiling effect on respiratory depression.
key_points: Buprenorphine displaces full agonists because of its higher receptor affinity
Induction is timed by objective withdrawal features, not hours since last use
Long-acting opioids require a longer wait than short-acting ones
Subjective distress alone does not confirm readiness for the first dose
The ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes maintenance safer than methadone
explanation.pearls: Precipitated withdrawal from a too early buprenorphine dose can last many hours and is the single commonest reason a patient refuses to attempt opioid replacement again, so the wait for objective signs is a retention issue as much as a comfort one.

options.rationale: The interval alone is not sufficient for a slow release preparation, whose duration of action extends well beyond that of immediate release opioids. The objective score rather than the clock determines readiness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Symptomatic cover does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, which can be severe and prolonged and frequently causes patients to disengage from treatment. The timing problem is not solved pharmacologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Buprenorphine has high receptor affinity with partial agonist activity, so giving it while substantial full agonist still occupies the receptor displaces that agonist and precipitates withdrawal. Waiting until objective withdrawal is established confirms the receptor is sufficiently free. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Switching agent avoids the timing issue but commits him to a drug with a narrower safety margin during induction and greater overdose risk. His preference and circumstances have not been shown to favour it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Naloxone would itself precipitate severe withdrawal and has no role in planned induction. It is used for opioid overdose with respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur between six and forty eight hours after the last drink, are generalised tonic clonic, and usually occur singly or in a short cluster without focal features. A first seizure in this context still warrants imaging and biochemical assessment, since head injury, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance are common in this population and can coexist. Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice because they restore the inhibitory tone lost when chronic alcohol exposure is withdrawn, and conventional antiepileptic drugs do not prevent recurrence. A loading or front loaded regimen with a long-acting agent gives immediate protection and a pharmacologically smooth taper, and is preferred to symptom triggered dosing once a seizure has occurred. Thiamine is given parenterally before any carbohydrate load, and having had a withdrawal seizure identifies a patient at higher risk of progressing to delirium tremens, which warrants closer observation over the following days.
key_points: Withdrawal seizures occur six to forty eight hours after the last drink
Benzodiazepines prevent recurrence and antiepileptic drugs do not
Loading with a long-acting agent is preferred once a seizure has occurred
Parenteral thiamine precedes any glucose administration
A withdrawal seizure predicts higher risk of later delirium tremens
explanation.pearls: Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine to a chronically alcohol dependent patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so parenteral thiamine goes in first even when the blood glucose is low.

options.rationale: Antiepileptic drugs are ineffective for withdrawal seizures because the mechanism is receptor mediated central nervous system hyperexcitability rather than an epileptic focus. They are indicated when an independent seizure disorder coexists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Carbamazepine has some role in mild withdrawal in ambulatory settings in other countries but is not the Australian approach and is not adequate after a seizure. Benzodiazepine cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and would increase the risk of a further seizure. They are used only as an adjunct for hallucinations once benzodiazepine cover is adequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Long-acting benzodiazepines are the only agents shown to prevent recurrent withdrawal seizures, and diazepam self tapers through its active metabolites. Parenteral thiamine precedes glucose because a glucose load in a thiamine deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

A symptom triggered threshold approach is reasonable for uncomplicated withdrawal but is inadequate once a seizure has occurred, since the seizure marks a higher risk course. Front loading provides immediate protection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Separating a substance induced psychotic disorder from a primary psychotic illness that has been unmasked or accompanied by substance use is one of the harder judgements in general psychiatry, and it usually cannot be made at a single point in time. The course of symptoms during confirmed abstinence is the most useful guide, since a genuinely substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks once the drug is cleared. Features favouring a primary disorder include symptoms persisting well beyond that window, a premorbid decline in function preceding the substance use, prominent negative symptoms, and a family history of psychotic illness. A substantial proportion of people given an initial diagnosis of methamphetamine induced psychosis are later rediagnosed with schizophrenia, so the safest position early on is to treat the symptoms, verify abstinence objectively, and let the longitudinal course clarify the diagnosis rather than committing prematurely in either direction.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks of abstinence
Persistence well beyond that window favours a primary psychotic illness
Premorbid functional decline before substance use is a key historical clue
Objectively verified abstinence is needed before the course can be interpreted
Many initial substance induced diagnoses are later revised to schizophrenia
explanation.pearls: Psychotic symptoms that persist beyond about one month of objectively verified abstinence from methamphetamine should shift the working diagnosis towards a primary psychotic illness, and the premorbid year is often where the answer already lies.

options.rationale: Symptoms that have already outlasted a month of abstinence are unlikely to be purely substance induced, and stopping treatment risks deterioration. Resolution within days to weeks is the expected pattern for a substance induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Committing to a lifelong diagnosis at this point overstates the certainty available and can be difficult to revise once documented. The duration criterion and longitudinal course still need to be established. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Treatment resistance requires failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials of sufficient dose and duration, and he has had only one. An adequate trial is generally considered to be at least four to six weeks at therapeutic dose. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Psychosis persisting more than a month beyond confirmed abstinence exceeds the expected course of a substance induced disorder and raises the likelihood of a primary psychotic illness, particularly given the premorbid decline his family describes. Continuing treatment while observing over time is the approach that avoids both premature labelling and undertreatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

Autoimmune encephalitis is suggested by confusion, seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability or a fluctuating conscious state, none of which is present. His examination and course do not fit that pattern. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis and occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and a wide range of medical and neurological conditions, with mood disorders the commonest psychiatric association. It is frequently missed because the immobile, mute patient is assumed to be depressed, uncooperative or sedated, and because clinicians look for a rigid patient rather than one with waxy flexibility and preserved alertness. Recognition rests on identifying several signs from the characteristic cluster, which includes stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypy. A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both treatment and diagnostic test, while antipsychotics should be withheld because they can precipitate malignant catatonia, which overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and carries high mortality. Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail, and the medical complications of immobility and poor intake, including dehydration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration, need active management throughout.
key_points: Catatonia is a syndrome seen most often with mood disorders, not only psychosis
Waxy flexibility with preserved alertness distinguishes it from a sedated patient
A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both first line treatment and a diagnostic test
Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and are withheld
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when benzodiazepines fail
explanation.pearls: A mildly raised creatine kinase without fever or rigidity reflects immobility in catatonia rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and mistaking one for the other sends the patient to dantrolene instead of the lorazepam that would have worked.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic therapy in catatonia risks converting it to the malignant form with hyperthermia and autonomic instability. The drug is a plausible contributor rather than the solution. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: This treats neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which requires fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and a markedly raised creatine kinase. She has none of these and her tone is not rigid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective and is the definitive treatment where the benzodiazepine trial fails or the malignant form develops, but a lorazepam challenge comes first. Sequencing rather than efficacy is the issue. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: The combination of mutism, waxy flexibility, negativism and echolalia establishes catatonia, for which a benzodiazepine challenge is both the first line treatment and diagnostically informative. The antipsychotic is withheld because it can worsen catatonia and precipitate the malignant form. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Investigation for an organic cause is reasonable in parallel but should not delay a treatment that is safe, rapidly acting and diagnostically useful. Her known mood disorder and classic signs make catatonia the leading diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Lithium acts on the collecting duct to reduce the responsiveness of the tubule to antidiuretic hormone, producing a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that affects a substantial minority of long term users. It presents with polyuria and compensatory thirst, is related to duration of therapy rather than to the serum level, and is therefore easily dismissed when the level comes back within range. The critical hazard is that the patient depends on continuous access to water, so any illness, surgery, fasting or heat stress that interrupts drinking can produce rapid hypernatraemic dehydration, which in turn reduces lithium clearance and precipitates toxicity. Diagnosis is by demonstrating an inappropriately dilute urine in the face of a high normal or raised serum sodium. Management involves renal input, ensuring unrestricted fluid access, considering amiloride which blocks the epithelial sodium channel through which lithium enters the tubular cell, and weighing whether to continue lithium against the difficulty of replacing it in a patient whose mood has been stable for years.
key_points: Lithium causes nephrogenic rather than central diabetes insipidus
Risk relates to duration of exposure, not to the serum level
Inappropriately dilute urine with high normal sodium confirms the diagnosis
Interrupted access to water can cause rapid hypernatraemia and lithium toxicity
Amiloride has a rational basis where desmopressin does not
explanation.pearls: A patient with lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus who is made nil by mouth for surgery can become dangerously hypernatraemic within hours, so the perioperative fluid plan matters more than the lithium level.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: This complication occurs at therapeutic levels and relates to cumulative duration of exposure rather than concentration, so a normal level offers no reassurance. It also carries a real risk of dangerous dehydration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A dilute urine despite a high normal serum sodium indicates a failure of renal concentrating ability rather than excessive drinking, and paired osmolality demonstrates this objectively. Renal involvement guides whether lithium can continue and how the kidney is monitored. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Restricting fluid in a patient who cannot concentrate urine risks rapid hypernatraemic dehydration and lithium toxicity. His high normal sodium already indicates he is only just keeping pace. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

The defect is renal resistance to antidiuretic hormone rather than a deficiency of it, so exogenous hormone is largely ineffective. Amiloride is the agent with a rational basis in this setting. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

His glucose and glycated haemoglobin already exclude diabetes mellitus, and a water deprivation test is potentially hazardous here without renal supervision. Paired osmolality is the safer first measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Bipolar depression accounts for far more of the illness burden over a lifetime than mania does, yet it is treated differently from unipolar depression and the distinction is frequently missed when a patient presents during a depressed phase and does not volunteer a past manic episode. The central concern is that antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate a switch into mania, induce rapid cycling, or produce a mixed state, with the risk greatest in bipolar I disorder and with noradrenergic agents. Australian guidance therefore favours quetiapine, lurasidone, or lamotrigine, with olanzapine combined with fluoxetine as an alternative, rather than an antidepressant alone. Where an antidepressant is used it should be given under the cover of an adequate mood stabiliser and withdrawn once the episode resolves. Every depressed patient should be asked directly about past periods of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep and uncharacteristic risk taking, since the history determines the treatment far more than the current presentation does.
key_points: Bipolar depression causes more lifetime burden than mania and is treated differently
Antidepressant monotherapy risks manic switch, mixed states and rapid cycling
Quetiapine, lurasidone and lamotrigine are preferred first line options
Any antidepressant used should be covered by an adequate mood stabiliser
Ask every depressed patient directly about past elevated mood
explanation.pearls: Switch risk in bipolar I disorder is highest with noradrenergic antidepressants such as venlafaxine and with tricyclics, which is why an unopposed serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the least defensible of the antidepressant options.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: An antidepressant without mood stabilising cover carries a recognised risk of switching him into mania or inducing rapid cycling, particularly given his bipolar I history. Antidepressants are not first line for bipolar depression. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors carry a higher switch risk than other antidepressant classes and the same objection applies with greater force. Noradrenergic agents are the least suitable choice here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Lithium is excellent for maintenance and reduces suicide risk but has more modest acute antidepressant effect, so it is slower to address the current episode. It is a reasonable addition once he has recovered. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct but is not sufficient alone for a moderate to severe bipolar depressive episode with functional impairment and passive suicidal thoughts. He also currently has no prophylactic cover. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Quetiapine has the strongest evidence for bipolar depression and treats the episode while providing mood stabilising cover against a switch to mania. Monotherapy avoids the risk carried by an unopposed antidepressant in a patient with a documented manic episode. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by a dementia with fluctuating cognition, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and it is commonly misdiagnosed as Alzheimer disease or delirium. Recognising it matters because of severe neuroleptic sensitivity, in which a standard dose of an antipsychotic can cause profound rigidity, sedation, autonomic instability and a marked rise in mortality. Management of behavioural symptoms therefore begins with identifying and removing contributors such as pain, infection, constipation and anticholinergic drugs, and with environmental and carer directed strategies. Cholinesterase inhibitors have better evidence in this condition than in most other dementias and can improve both cognition and hallucinations. If an antipsychotic becomes unavoidable for severe distress or risk, quetiapine at the lowest possible dose is generally preferred, with explicit discussion of the mortality risk and a defined review date.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment define the syndrome
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity can follow even a single standard antipsychotic dose
Reversible contributors such as pain, infection and anticholinergics are addressed first
Cholinesterase inhibitors have better evidence here than in other dementias
Levodopa improves motor features but worsens hallucinations
explanation.pearls: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder often precedes the cognitive decline of dementia with Lewy bodies by years, so a partner's account of dream enactment is frequently the detail that prevents a catastrophic antipsychotic prescription.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Marked antipsychotic sensitivity in this condition means even low doses can cause severe parkinsonism, sedation and a rise in mortality, so drug treatment is not the starting point. Environmental strategies and removal of aggravating drugs address the distress with far less risk. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: This is among the least suitable choices because severe sensitivity reactions are well recognised with this class in this condition. It would be a more defensible option in Alzheimer dementia after non-drug measures failed. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: A typical antipsychotic carries the greatest risk of a severe sensitivity reaction and can produce irreversible deterioration. Its use in this setting is specifically cautioned against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A long-acting benzodiazepine increases falls, confusion and daytime sedation in an older man who has already fallen twice. It treats none of the underlying features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
