Dopaminergic therapy may help the motor features but characteristically worsens visual hallucinations, which are his main behavioural problem. It is introduced cautiously only once behavioural symptoms are controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: This presentation requires three separate errors to be recognised at once. First, lithium levels are only interpretable as twelve hour trough samples, so a level drawn six hours after a dose sits on the descending limb of absorption and understates the trough, meaning a reported 1.1 mmol/L represents a considerably higher true burden. Second, both perindopril and hydrochlorothiazide reduce lithium clearance, the thiazide by increasing proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption and the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor by reducing glomerular filtration, and their combination has produced an acute kidney injury that will drive further accumulation. Third, chronic toxicity causes neurological injury at far lower levels than acute overdose because lithium has already equilibrated into the central nervous system, so the severity of the clinical syndrome rather than the serum number determines management. Treatment is cessation of lithium and the interacting drugs, volume repletion with sodium chloride to restore clearance, and early renal consultation, since haemodialysis is indicated for severe neurological features or impaired renal clearance irrespective of whether the level crosses a particular threshold.
key_points: Lithium levels are interpretable only as twelve hour trough samples
Thiazides and renin angiotensin blockers both reduce lithium clearance
Chronic toxicity injures the brain at far lower levels than acute overdose
Clinical severity, not the serum number, drives the decision to dialyse
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and has no role
explanation.pearls: Haemodialysis in lithium toxicity is driven by neurological severity and renal function rather than by a level threshold, and a rebound rise several hours after dialysis as lithium redistributes out of tissue means a repeat level is always needed afterwards.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Simple observation is adequate for mild toxicity with normal renal function, but her acute kidney injury means the drug will continue to accumulate rather than clear. Waiting allows the neurological injury to progress. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Charcoal does not bind lithium at all, and gut decontamination has no role in chronic accumulation where the burden is already distributed to tissue. These measures address acute ingestion of a modified release preparation. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

A level drawn six hours post dose understates the trough, so 1.1 mmol/L here represents substantially greater toxicity than the number suggests, and the neurological signs with acute kidney injury define severe chronic toxicity. Volume repletion restores clearance while the renal team assesses the threshold for extracorporeal removal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Removing the interacting diuretic is correct but continuing any lithium in the setting of established neurotoxicity with acute kidney injury is unsafe. The timeframe also fails to match the severity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Urinary alkalinisation enhances elimination of weak acids such as salicylate, and lithium clearance is governed by sodium and volume status rather than by urine pH. The principle is misapplied to this drug. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of metabolic disturbances that follows the reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, and hypophosphataemia is its defining feature. During starvation the body depletes intracellular phosphate, magnesium and potassium while serum levels remain deceptively normal, and when carbohydrate is reintroduced the resulting insulin surge drives these ions into cells along with glucose, producing a rapid fall in serum concentrations that can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and death. Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of minimal intake, recent weight loss and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, and this patient is at high risk on several counts. Contemporary practice has shifted away from cautious underfeeding, which carries its own mortality, towards starting adequate nutrition while monitoring electrolytes at least daily and supplementing phosphate and thiamine prophylactically in high risk patients. Thiamine is given before or with the first feed because carbohydrate metabolism consumes it and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
key_points: Serum electrolytes are deceptively normal during starvation despite intracellular depletion
The insulin surge after carbohydrate drives phosphate into cells within days
Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of intake and recent weight loss
Prophylactic supplementation is preferred to reacting to a fallen level
Underfeeding is itself harmful and is no longer the recommended precaution
explanation.pearls: Thiamine must be given before or alongside the first feed in a severely malnourished patient, because the carbohydrate load consumes remaining thiamine stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within days of starting nutrition.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Waiting for the level to fall means treating an established deficiency that can already have caused cardiac and respiratory compromise. The admission level offers no reassurance because the fall occurs after feeding starts. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Her prolonged starvation and very low body mass index place her at high risk, and the phosphate falls only once feeding begins and insulin drives it intracellularly. Prophylactic supplementation alongside daily measurement prevents the fall rather than reacting to it. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: This frequency will miss the rapid fall that characteristically occurs within the first seventy two hours of feeding. Monitoring interval is as important as the decision to monitor. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Withholding nutrition in a severely malnourished patient carries its own mortality and does not reduce the risk once feeding eventually starts. Underfeeding is now recognised as a harm in its own right. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: A high carbohydrate load is the strongest driver of the intracellular shift and would increase rather than reduce the risk. Carbohydrate content is deliberately moderated during the early phase. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Stimulant treatment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is effective but requires a structured baseline assessment because the drugs raise heart rate and blood pressure and are subject to misuse and diversion. Routine baseline assessment comprises pulse, blood pressure, weight, a cardiovascular history and examination, and a review of substance use and any comorbid psychiatric illness. Routine electrocardiography is not required for everyone, which makes it important to recognise the specific features that do warrant cardiac referral: a personal history of structural heart disease, exertional chest pain, palpitations or syncope, an abnormal examination, or a family history of sudden unexplained death in a first degree relative under about forty years of age. In Australia, stimulant prescribing is additionally regulated at state level with authority requirements, and ongoing monitoring includes pulse, blood pressure and weight at each dose change and periodically thereafter. Comorbid substance use disorder does not preclude treatment but influences the choice of a longer acting or less divertible preparation.
key_points: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so baseline observations are mandatory
Routine electrocardiography is not required for every patient
Sudden unexplained death in a young first degree relative warrants cardiac referral
Non-stimulant alternatives do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment
State authority requirements apply to stimulant prescribing in Australia
explanation.pearls: A first degree relative who died suddenly and unexplained before about forty is the family history detail that converts a routine stimulant baseline into a cardiology referral, because inherited cardiomyopathies and channelopathies are often silent on examination.

options.rationale: Baseline observations are necessary for every patient but are insufficient here, because a normal examination does not exclude an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy. The family history changes the threshold for investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Substance use is worth assessing because of diversion and misuse risk, but he reports none and this does not address the cardiac question. It would not detect the risk that matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Non-stimulant agents also raise heart rate and blood pressure and do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment where the history warrants it. Changing drug class does not resolve the concern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

An unexplained sudden death in a first degree relative under fifty raises the possibility of an inherited cardiac condition and is the specific trigger for cardiac assessment rather than routine baseline observations alone. Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so this must be resolved before treatment begins. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Thyroid testing is not a routine requirement before stimulant treatment and would be prompted by clinical features of thyroid disease. It does not address the inherited cardiac risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Grief and depression overlap substantially in their surface features, since sadness, tearfulness, disturbed sleep, reduced appetite and weight loss occur in both, and the distinction rests on qualitative features rather than on symptom counting. In uncomplicated grief the dysphoria comes in waves triggered by reminders, with preserved capacity for pleasure and connection between those waves, whereas depression produces a persistent and pervasive lowering of mood with global anhedonia. Self esteem is characteristically preserved in grief, while worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the death and self loathing point to depression, and fleeting perceptual experiences of the deceased person are common in bereavement and are not psychotic. Any active suicidal ideation, marked psychomotor retardation, or persistent functional collapse should prompt treatment for depression. Prolonged grief disorder is a separate diagnosis requiring persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with functional impairment beyond six to twelve months, and it responds to specific psychological therapy rather than to antidepressants.
key_points: Grief produces waves of dysphoria with preserved reactivity between them
Depression produces persistent pervasive low mood with global anhedonia
Preserved self worth favours grief while worthlessness and guilt favour depression
Fleeting perceptions of the deceased are common and not psychotic
Prolonged grief disorder requires impairment beyond six to twelve months
explanation.pearls: Active suicidal ideation with a wish to die rather than a passive wish to be with the deceased is the feature that should move a bereaved patient out of the grief category and into treatment for depression, irrespective of how recent the loss was.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Antidepressants have not been shown to benefit uncomplicated grief and medicalising a normal process can undermine it. They are indicated if a depressive episode emerges. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Sedatives risk dependence, falls and confusion in an older person and do not address the underlying process. Broken sleep is an expected feature of early bereavement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Hearing the deceased person's voice while falling asleep is a recognised and benign feature of bereavement rather than a psychotic symptom. Treating it would expose her to significant risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Urgent specialist referral is reserved for suicidal ideation, psychotic depression, severe functional decline or failure to eat and drink, none of which is present. Her presentation can be managed in primary care with review. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Her reactivity of mood, preserved self worth, absent suicidal ideation and comforting rather than distressing perceptual experiences are characteristic of uncomplicated grief rather than a depressive episode. Planned review allows a depressive illness to be identified if the pattern changes. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder is chosen by matching the drug to the patient's stated goal rather than by ranking the drugs against each other in the abstract. Naltrexone reduces the reinforcing effect of alcohol and therefore reduces heavy drinking days, which makes it the agent of choice when the goal is reduced consumption or when the person is still drinking at the point of prescribing. Acamprosate stabilises glutamatergic transmission after withdrawal and is used to maintain an abstinence that has already been achieved, so it presupposes a completed withdrawal. Disulfiram requires both a firm abstinence goal and supervision to be safe and effective. All three sit alongside psychosocial support rather than replacing it, and a stated harm reduction goal is a legitimate clinical target rather than a failure of motivation.
key_points: Naltrexone reduces heavy drinking and does not require prior abstinence
Acamprosate maintains an abstinence that has already been achieved
Disulfiram requires a committed abstinence goal and supervised dosing
Concurrent opioid use contraindicates naltrexone and must be asked about
Pharmacotherapy supplements rather than replaces psychosocial treatment
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone will precipitate withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks opioid analgesia, so document a plan for acute pain and advise the patient to carry that information before the first dose.

sources.label: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Acamprosate works by maintaining abstinence once it has been achieved and requires the patient to have stopped drinking first, which he has declined to do. It has little effect on the quantity consumed in someone still drinking. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Disulfiram depends on an aversive reaction to any alcohol at all and therefore requires a committed abstinence goal with supervision, making it unsuitable for someone who intends to keep drinking. Using it here would risk a deliberate and dangerous reaction. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Naltrexone blocks the opioid mediated reward of drinking and reduces heavy drinking days and the quantity consumed, so it suits a harm reduction goal and does not require prior abstinence. His mildly raised transaminases with preserved synthetic function are not a contraindication, and he uses no opioids. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Baclofen is a later option used mainly where liver disease precludes the first line agents, and the evidence for it is weaker with a risk of sedation and of a withdrawal syndrome on abrupt cessation. His liver function does not force that choice. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Topiramate has some supporting evidence but is not registered for this indication in Australia and carries cognitive slowing and paraesthesiae that limit tolerability. It sits behind the established first line agents. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity arises when serotonergic agents are combined, and tramadol added to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is one of the commonest precipitants in Australian practice because the analgesic role of tramadol obscures its serotonergic action. The Hunter criteria diagnose it on the presence of a serotonergic agent with spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or hypertonia with hyperthermia and clonus. The lower limb predominance of clonus and hyperreflexia distinguishes it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which produces generalised lead-pipe rigidity with reduced reflexes over a slower onset. Management is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care, with cyproheptadine added when hyperthermia persists and intubation with paralysis reserved for temperatures above about 39.5 degrees.
key_points: Tramadol with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor is a common Australian precipitant
Clonus and hyperreflexia predominate in the lower limbs
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome shows rigidity with reduced reflexes instead
Benzodiazepines, cooling and drug withdrawal are the first measures
Cyproheptadine is added when hyperthermia persists despite those measures
explanation.pearls: Temperature above 39.5 degrees in serotonin toxicity is an indication for intubation with neuromuscular paralysis, because muscular hyperactivity is generating the heat and antipyretics are useless against it.

options.rationale: Dantrolene uncouples excitation from contraction in skeletal muscle and is used for malignant hyperthermia, where rigidity is the source of heat production. There is no evidence of benefit in serotonin toxicity and it does not address the receptor overactivity driving this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and a slower onset over days rather than the hyperreflexia and clonus seen here. Giving a dopamine agonist in serotonin toxicity may worsen it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Benzodiazepines remain the backbone of treatment and should continue, but escalating them alone after an inadequate response leaves the serotonin receptor overactivity unopposed. Persistent hyperthermia above 38.5 degrees is the trigger to add a specific antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Cyproheptadine is a serotonin receptor antagonist and is the specific treatment when toxicity persists despite withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines and cooling. It is given enterally, by nasogastric tube if necessary, and repeated until the agitation and clonus settle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Physostigmine is the antidote for central anticholinergic toxicity, which produces dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds and urinary retention rather than the diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel sounds of serotonin toxicity. The clonus here points firmly away from an anticholinergic cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome is increasingly common as cannabis potency rises, and it is repeatedly misdiagnosed because the association seems counterintuitive given that cannabinoids are used therapeutically as antiemetics. The clinical signature is a cyclical pattern of severe vomiting with entirely well intervals, in a long term heavy user, with compulsive hot bathing that the patient often does not mention unless asked directly. Standard antiemetics work poorly, whereas topical capsaicin gives symptomatic relief through the same transient receptor potential vanilloid pathway that hot water stimulates, and benzodiazepines are sometimes used in the acute phase. Resolution requires complete cessation rather than reduction, and symptoms may take several weeks to settle after stopping, which should be explained in advance or the patient will conclude that cannabis was not the cause.
key_points: Episodic vomiting with well intervals in a heavy long term user is the pattern
Compulsive hot bathing is close to pathognomonic but must be asked about
Conventional antiemetics are characteristically ineffective
Topical capsaicin acts on the same receptor pathway as hot water
Only complete cessation resolves it, and symptoms may take weeks to settle
explanation.pearls: Warn patients that vomiting may continue for several weeks after stopping cannabis, because a premature return to use during that lag is the commonest reason the diagnosis is rejected by the patient.

options.rationale: Conventional antiemetics including ondansetron characteristically perform poorly in this syndrome, and fluids treat the consequence while the cause continues. Supportive care has a place during an acute episode but is not the answer to a recurring pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Acid suppression addresses reflux or ulcer disease, and his gastroscopy has already excluded both. Repeating an investigation that was normal is unlikely to yield a different result in the absence of new features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Tricyclic prophylaxis is used in idiopathic cyclical vomiting syndrome, which shares the episodic pattern but lacks the relationship to heavy cannabis use and the compulsive hot bathing behaviour. The distinction matters because removing the cannabis resolves this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Motility studies are directed at gastroparesis, which produces persistent rather than episodic symptoms with complete well intervals, and further investigation after a normal endoscopic and imaging workup delays effective treatment. The history here is already characteristic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Episodic vomiting with complete recovery between attacks, relieved specifically by compulsive hot bathing in a daily cannabis user, is diagnostic, and complete cessation is the only intervention that reliably resolves it. Topical capsaicin applied to the abdomen acts on the same receptor pathway as the hot water and provides symptomatic relief during an acute episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults is associated with a measurably higher rate of motor vehicle crashes, driven by inattention, impulsivity and risk taking, and pharmacological treatment reduces that excess risk rather than adding to it. The Australian fitness to drive standards therefore do not treat the diagnosis or its treatment as automatically disqualifying, and a stable adult on established therapy with an unremarkable driving record is generally fit for a private licence. The legal duty to report a long term condition that may affect driving sits with the licence holder, while the treating doctor advises the patient, documents that advice, and notifies the licensing authority directly only when a patient continues to drive unsafely against that advice. Commercial licence holders are assessed against a more demanding standard, and stimulant misuse or diversion, substance use disorder and untreated symptoms are the features that actually raise concern.
key_points: Untreated symptoms raise crash risk while effective treatment lowers it
Neither the diagnosis nor stimulant treatment is automatically disqualifying
The duty to notify the licensing authority rests with the driver
Direct medical notification is reserved for continued unsafe driving against advice
Commercial licence holders are assessed against a stricter standard
explanation.pearls: Document the specific advice given about driving and the patient's obligation to notify, because that contemporaneous note is what protects the clinician if a crash later occurs.

options.rationale: Treatment improves rather than impairs driving performance in this condition, so ceasing it would raise his crash risk rather than lower it. Blanket driving restriction is not supported by the Australian fitness to drive standards for a stable treated patient. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

Withholding the medication on driving days removes the symptom control that reduces his crash risk and is the opposite of what the evidence supports. Drug holidays are sometimes discussed for appetite or growth reasons in children, not for driving safety. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

Untreated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with a higher crash rate, and stimulant treatment reduces it, so a stable well controlled patient with no adverse driving history is generally fit to drive. Recording that the discussion took place, including the duty to report any condition affecting driving, is the appropriate action in general practice. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

The obligation to notify rests primarily with the driver, and a doctor reporting directly is reserved for situations where the patient continues to drive against advice despite a condition that makes it unsafe. Bypassing the conversation damages the relationship without any safety gain here. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

Changing an effective and well tolerated treatment introduces a period of poorer symptom control, during which his driving risk would rise. Non stimulant agents are chosen for tolerability, misuse risk or comorbidity rather than to satisfy a driving requirement. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: The boundary between schizoaffective disorder and a mood disorder with psychotic features is drawn by the temporal relationship between psychosis and mood, not by the content or severity of either. In bipolar disorder with psychotic features the psychotic symptoms occur only within mood episodes and remit as the mood normalises, whereas schizoaffective disorder requires a period of at least two weeks in which delusions or hallucinations persist without a major mood episode. A second requirement prevents the diagnosis drifting towards schizophrenia: mood episodes must be present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. Making the distinction properly requires longitudinal information, which is why mood charts and collateral history carry more weight than any single cross sectional assessment, and it matters because it shapes long term prognosis and the balance between mood stabilising and antipsychotic treatment.
key_points: Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features
Schizoaffective disorder requires two weeks of psychosis without a major mood episode
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total illness duration
Longitudinal data and collateral history are needed for the distinction
Substance use and thyroid disease must be excluded before the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A mood chart maintained over months is the single most useful diagnostic instrument here, because the diagnosis turns on whether psychosis and mood disturbance overlap in time rather than on any feature visible at a single interview.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Mood congruent delusions during a manic episode are entirely typical of bipolar disorder with psychotic features and do not distinguish between the two diagnoses. Their presence is expected in both. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: The defining requirement is psychotic symptoms lasting two weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode, while mood symptoms are present for the majority of the illness overall. His documented six to eight week euthymic stretches with continuing hallucinations and delusions satisfy exactly this criterion. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Family history informs risk but does not determine which diagnosis applies to an individual, and the genetic contributions to schizoaffective and bipolar disorder overlap substantially. It cannot settle the distinction. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Treatment response is not a diagnostic criterion, and incomplete response to monotherapy occurs across both conditions. Reasoning backwards from a drug response is a recognised source of diagnostic error. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Early adult onset is the typical age of presentation for both conditions and for schizophrenia, so it carries no discriminating value. Age alone never separates these diagnoses. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: Severe hyponatraemia after recreational stimulant use arises from two mechanisms acting together: the drug stimulates antidiuretic hormone release, and public health messages about overheating prompt users to drink large volumes of water that they then cannot excrete. Young women appear disproportionately affected, and the presentation is confusion, headache, vomiting or seizures rather than anything that points obviously to sodium. The urgency comes from cerebral oedema in a skull that cannot accommodate it, and the treatment principle is that symptomatic hyponatraemia is corrected quickly at first and slowly thereafter. A rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L usually stops seizures, after which the total correction is limited to around 8 mmol/L in any 24 hour period to avoid osmotic demyelination, a delayed and often irreversible syndrome of quadriparesis and bulbar failure.
key_points: Stimulant induced antidiuretic hormone release plus water loading causes the fall
Seizures or reduced consciousness make this an emergency requiring hypertonic saline
An initial rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L is enough to relieve cerebral oedema
Limit total correction to about 8 mmol/L in 24 hours
Normal saline can worsen the sodium when antidiuretic hormone release persists
explanation.pearls: Osmotic demyelination appears two to six days after over rapid correction, not at the time, so the sodium must be rechecked every two hours during treatment and the rise capped even when the patient looks better.

options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the treatment for mild or asymptomatic dilutional hyponatraemia and works far too slowly for a patient who has already had a seizure. Cerebral oedema at this sodium level requires active correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Normal saline is relatively hypotonic against this degree of hyponatraemia and, where antidiuretic hormone release persists, the sodium can be excreted while the water is retained, paradoxically lowering the level further. It is not the fluid for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

The problem is an excess of free water rather than a deficit, so giving more dextrose solution would deepen the hyponatraemia and worsen cerebral oedema. This is the opposite of the required intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Hyponatraemia with seizures or a reduced conscious state is a neurological emergency requiring hypertonic saline in small repeated boluses, aiming to raise the sodium by about 4 to 6 mmol/L quickly, which is enough to relieve cerebral oedema. Correction is then slowed and capped to avoid osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Oral supplementation is unreliable in a drowsy patient with an unprotected airway and acts far too slowly for a seizure related emergency. It has a role in chronic mild hyponatraemia instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Women with bipolar I disorder face their highest lifetime risk of relapse in the weeks after birth, with postpartum psychosis occurring in a substantial minority of those who stop prophylaxis, so maintaining an effective mood stabiliser is the dominant consideration in perinatal planning. Lithium is excreted into breast milk and the neonatal glomerular filtration rate is low, which historically led to blanket advice against breastfeeding. Contemporary Australian guidance takes a case by case approach, supporting breastfeeding for a healthy term infant when maternal levels are stable, the infant is monitored with lithium levels alongside renal and thyroid function, and the parents understand the signs of infant toxicity such as poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia and jitteriness. The main practical hazard is infant dehydration during an intercurrent illness, which concentrates lithium and can precipitate toxicity quickly. Sleep protection, a written relapse plan and continuity with a perinatal service matter as much as the drug decision.
key_points: Postpartum relapse risk in bipolar I disorder is the highest of any life stage
Lithium enters breast milk and neonatal renal clearance is limited
Breastfeeding is acceptable in a healthy term infant with scheduled monitoring
Infant dehydration during illness is the main precipitant of toxicity
Valproate is avoided in women of reproductive age wherever possible
explanation.pearls: Teach the parents that poor feeding, lethargy, jitteriness or hypotonia in the baby warrant an urgent infant lithium level, and that any illness causing dehydration is a reason to seek review the same day.

options.rationale: Lithium was historically treated as an absolute contraindication, but current Australian guidance regards breastfeeding as acceptable in a healthy term infant with adequate monitoring. An absolute prohibition also carries its own harm through the loss of breastfeeding benefits and the effect on maternal mood. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

Lithium does pass into breast milk in measurable amounts and the neonatal kidney clears it slowly, so unmonitored feeding is not appropriate. The monitoring is what makes the choice safe rather than an optional extra. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

In a healthy term infant with an alert mother and good support, breastfeeding can be supported provided the baby has scheduled lithium levels along with renal and thyroid function, and the parents are taught the signs of toxicity. Dehydration in the infant is the main hazard, since it concentrates lithium, so any illness with poor feeding triggers earlier review. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

Valproate is avoided in women of reproductive age wherever possible because of its teratogenic and neurodevelopmental effects in any future pregnancy, and switching a stable patient postpartum risks relapse at the highest risk time of her life. It is the wrong drug to move towards. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

The early postpartum period carries the highest lifetime risk of relapse and of postpartum psychosis in bipolar I disorder, so stopping effective prophylaxis now is the most dangerous option available. Maintaining the mood stabiliser protects both mother and infant. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

explanation.summary: The ultra high risk or at risk mental state describes young people with attenuated psychotic symptoms, brief self-limiting psychotic episodes, or a genetic risk combined with recent functional decline, and it was developed largely through Australian research. Attenuated symptoms differ from frank psychosis in that insight is retained and the beliefs are held with doubt rather than conviction, which is the distinction that determines management. Roughly one in five will transition to a first episode of psychosis within two years, and many of the remainder have persistent depressive, anxiety or functional problems that deserve treatment regardless. Guidelines recommend cognitive behavioural therapy with regular structured monitoring, treatment of comorbid depression or anxiety, psychoeducation and support to maintain education or employment, while reserving antipsychotic medication for those who transition or whose symptoms are severe and unresponsive. Antipsychotics have not demonstrated a preventive effect and carry metabolic consequences that matter greatly over a lifetime.
key_points: Retained insight with doubt about the experiences distinguishes attenuated symptoms
Functional decline plus family history contributes to the risk designation
About one in five transition to frank psychosis within two years
Cognitive behavioural therapy with structured monitoring is first line
Antipsychotics are not preventive and are reserved for transition or severity
explanation.pearls: Duration of untreated psychosis is one of the few modifiable predictors of long term outcome in schizophrenia, which is why structured monitoring of an at risk young person is itself an active treatment rather than watchful waiting.

sources.label: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Antipsychotics have not been shown to prevent transition to psychosis in this group and expose a young person to metabolic and movement adverse effects, so they are not first line before frank psychosis develops. They are reserved for those who transition or who have severe unremitting symptoms despite psychological treatment. (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.rationale: He meets ultra high risk criteria through attenuated psychotic symptoms with retained insight plus functional decline and a first degree family history, and cognitive behavioural therapy with regular structured review is the recommended first line intervention. Monitoring matters because roughly a fifth transition to a first episode within two years and early detection shortens the duration of untreated psychosis. (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.rationale: Antidepressants are appropriate where a depressive or anxiety disorder is present and needs treatment in its own right, but no such syndrome is described here. Treating an absent condition delays the intervention that is indicated. (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.rationale: Discharge ignores six months of functional decline and a substantial transition risk, and it removes the monitoring that would detect deterioration early. Passive safety netting is insufficient when the functional trajectory is already downward. (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.rationale: There is no risk to himself or others and no acute crisis, so admission is disproportionate and carries its own harms through disruption and stigma at a formative age. Community based assessment and treatment is both sufficient and preferable. (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

explanation.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates and is caused by an underlying medical problem, and it complicates a large proportion of hip fracture admissions in older people. It is independently associated with longer stay, functional decline, institutionalisation, persistent cognitive impairment and mortality, so it is treated as a medical emergency rather than a behavioural problem. Management begins with a systematic search for contributors, captured by mnemonics covering pain, infection, constipation, urinary retention, medication, metabolic disturbance, hypoxia and sensory deprivation, and this case names three at once. Non-pharmacological measures are first line and include reorientation, family involvement, daylight and sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, hydration and restoring glasses and hearing aids. Antipsychotics neither shorten delirium nor prevent it, and are reserved for severe distress or risk that persists despite these measures, at the lowest dose and for the shortest period, with a documented plan for cessation.
key_points: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention with a medical cause
Retention, constipation, pain and opioids are common reversible contributors
Non-pharmacological measures are first line in every Australian guideline
Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and are reserved for severe distress
Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in withdrawal states
explanation.pearls: Hypoactive delirium is commoner than the hyperactive form and carries a worse prognosis, yet is routinely missed because a quiet withdrawn patient does not trigger a call, which is why formal attention testing beats relying on nursing concern.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Urinary retention of 620 mL, constipation and opioid exposure are three identified and correctable contributors, and relieving them addresses the cause rather than the behaviour. Non-pharmacological measures including reorientation, family presence, daylight exposure, glasses and hearing aids, and protected sleep are the recommended first line in every Australian delirium guideline. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium or improve outcomes and are reserved for severe distress or danger that persists despite non-pharmacological measures, used at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Prescribing regularly until discharge is exactly the pattern that leads to falls and continuation into the community. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people through disinhibition and sedation, and their use is confined to alcohol or sedative withdrawal delirium. There is no suggestion of withdrawal here. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Restraint increases agitation, injury, pressure injury and mortality, and is associated with prolonged delirium rather than resolution. Constant observation and environmental modification achieve the same safety aim without those harms. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Neuroimaging has a low yield in delirium without focal neurological signs, a history of head injury or anticoagulation, none of which applies. Moving a distressed patient to the scanner at night typically worsens the agitation while the treatable causes remain untreated. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist with a short duration of action of roughly 30 to 90 minutes, which is far shorter than that of many opioids and dramatically shorter than that of methadone, whose effects persist beyond 24 hours. The consequence is that a patient who wakes impressively after a bolus is not cured but temporarily antagonised, and respiratory depression recurs as the naloxone is cleared. Management therefore depends on identifying the agent: a short-acting opioid may need only a period of observation, while a long-acting agent requires a titrated naloxone infusion and prolonged monitoring, often in a high dependency setting. Naloxone is deliberately titrated to restore adequate ventilation rather than full consciousness, because overshooting precipitates acute withdrawal, agitation and absconding in a dependent patient. Every episode is also an opportunity for opioid treatment referral and for supplying take home naloxone with training for the patient and their household.
key_points: Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes while methadone persists beyond 24 hours
Waking after a bolus does not indicate the overdose has resolved
Long-acting opioid ingestion requires an infusion and prolonged observation
Titrate to adequate ventilation rather than full alertness
Arrange take home naloxone and treatment referral before eventual discharge
explanation.pearls: Start a naloxone infusion at roughly two thirds of the bolus dose that restored ventilation, given per hour, and titrate against respiratory rate rather than conscious level to avoid precipitating withdrawal.

options.rationale: His current normality reflects the naloxone rather than clearance of the opioid, and discharging him means he leaves as the antagonist wears off. Early discharge after reversal of a long-acting opioid is a recognised cause of death outside the department. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

A further bolus simply extends the same short window and may precipitate withdrawal, agitation and absconding, without addressing the mismatch in duration. Repeated boluses are an argument for an infusion rather than for discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Mental health legislation applies to treatment of a mental illness and is not the instrument for detaining someone who needs medical observation. Where a patient lacks capacity because of intoxication, treatment proceeds under common law or guardianship provisions, not the mental health act. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Naloxone has a duration of roughly 30 to 90 minutes whereas methadone acts for 24 hours or more, so recurrent respiratory depression is expected and a titrated infusion with prolonged monitored observation is required. The infusion is usually run at about two thirds of the effective waking bolus dose per hour and weaned against respiratory rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Take home naloxone is a valuable harm reduction measure to arrange before eventual discharge, but it depends on a bystander recognising and treating a future event and cannot substitute for observation during a current overdose. The risk period is now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Clozapine remains the only agent with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, and its monitoring framework is built almost entirely around agranulocytosis, which is the complication clinicians reliably remember. Gastrointestinal hypomotility is considerably more common and, on published case series, kills more patients, because clozapine has potent anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects that slow transit throughout the gut. The spectrum runs from ordinary constipation through faecal impaction to paralytic ileus, and then to bowel ischaemia, perforation and death, with the added difficulty that patients on clozapine often report symptoms late or poorly. Prevention is therefore active rather than reactive: bowel habit is asked about at every review, prophylactic aperients are commonly prescribed from the outset, and other constipating drugs are avoided where possible. An acute presentation with obstipation, vomiting, distension and absent bowel sounds is a surgical emergency requiring urgent imaging and combined stimulant and osmotic laxative treatment, not a psychiatric problem to be managed on the ward.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects slow transit throughout the gut
Progression runs from constipation to ileus, ischaemia and perforation
Myocarditis occurs in the first four to six weeks, not years into treatment
Prophylactic aperients and active bowel history taking are preventive standards
explanation.pearls: Ask about bowel habit at every clozapine review and prescribe a prophylactic aperient from initiation, because patients frequently do not volunteer constipation and the first presentation can be an established ileus.

options.rationale: Agranulocytosis is the adverse effect clinicians associate most strongly with clozapine and is the reason for mandatory monitoring, but it presents with fever, sore throat and infection rather than with an obstructed abdomen, and his neutrophils are normal. Anchoring on the familiar complication is what allows the gastrointestinal one to be missed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A softener alone is inadequate for six days of obstipation with vomiting and absent bowel sounds, and a week of further observation risks progression to ischaemia and perforation. Routine aperients are for prevention rather than for an acute obstructive presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Stopping the drug does not relieve an established ileus and risks rapid psychiatric relapse, with reinstatement then requiring retitration from a low dose. The immediate priority is to assess and treat the bowel rather than to withdraw the medication blindly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clozapine induced myocarditis is a genuine and serious complication, but it occurs characteristically in the first four to six weeks of treatment and presents with fever, tachycardia, chest pain and heart failure rather than with a distended silent abdomen. He is three years into treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clozapine induced gastrointestinal hypomotility results from potent anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects on the gut and can progress through ileus to bowel ischaemia, perforation and death, with a case fatality far exceeding that of agranulocytosis. Urgent imaging with surgical involvement and aggressive combined laxative therapy is required, alongside withholding other constipating agents. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release, so antipsychotics that block dopamine receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raise prolactin, with risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride the most potent offenders and aripiprazole notable for lowering it through partial agonism. The resulting syndrome of amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and, over time, reduced bone mineral density is frequently not volunteered by patients and not asked about by clinicians, yet it is a leading cause of covert non-adherence and therefore of relapse. Before attributing an elevation to the drug, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and other causative medications should be excluded, and stress or recent breast examination can produce modest transient rises. Imaging is reserved for levels disproportionate to the drug, usually taken as above roughly 2500 to 3000 mIU/L, or for mass effect symptoms such as headache or visual field loss. Where the elevation is symptomatic, switching to a prolactin sparing agent is preferred to adding a dopamine agonist, which works against the treatment itself.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin the most
Aripiprazole is a partial agonist that characteristically lowers prolactin
Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and other drugs first
Image when the level is disproportionate or there are mass effect symptoms
Long term elevation reduces bone mineral density and drives non-adherence
explanation.pearls: Sexual side effects and galactorrhoea are among the commonest reasons for silent antipsychotic non-adherence, so ask about periods, breast discharge and sexual function directly at review rather than waiting for them to be reported.

options.rationale: A dopamine agonist directly opposes the mechanism by which the antipsychotic works and risks precipitating psychotic relapse, so it is reserved for cases where the antipsychotic cannot be changed. It would also be a second drug added to treat the effect of the first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Imaging is indicated when the elevation is disproportionate to the drug, typically above about 2500 to 3000 mIU/L, or when there are headaches, visual field defects or other pituitary hormone abnormalities, none of which applies. A modest rise fully explained by a known cause does not require a scan before acting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Withdrawing treatment from a woman who has been stable for two years carries a high risk of relapse with loss of employment and independence. The problem is the choice of agent rather than the fact of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Restoring withdrawal bleeds masks the amenorrhoea and provides bone protection but leaves the galactorrhoea and the underlying elevation untreated, and does nothing about the adherence problem it is causing. It treats a consequence rather than the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Risperidone raises prolactin more than any other commonly used antipsychotic by blocking tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors, whereas aripiprazole is a partial agonist that characteristically lowers prolactin and frequently normalises it. Switching addresses the cause while maintaining antipsychotic cover, which matters here because the symptoms are already eroding her adherence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoids are full agonists at the cannabinoid receptor, unlike the partial agonism of plant cannabis, which is why they cause far more severe agitation, psychosis, tachycardia, hypertension, seizures and hyperthermia. They are not detected by standard urine drug screens, so a negative panel in a patient with a compatible history is uninformative rather than reassuring. Management is supportive: benzodiazepines for agitation and sympathomimetic features, a low stimulus environment, fluids, and monitoring for hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and acute kidney injury. Antipsychotics are reserved for agitation not controlled by benzodiazepines.
key_points: A negative urine drug screen does not exclude synthetic cannabinoid use
Benzodiazepines are first line; antipsychotics are second line because of seizure threshold, QT and thermoregulatory effects
Check creatine kinase, renal function and temperature for rhabdomyolysis and hyperthermia
Symptoms are usually self-limiting over hours, so ongoing antipsychotic treatment is not indicated
explanation.pearls: Recheck the creatine kinase before discharge rather than acting on the first value: rhabdomyolysis from prolonged agitation peaks 12 to 24 hours after presentation, and an initially modest result can rise substantially while the patient is being observed.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold, prolong the QT interval and impair heat dissipation, all of which matter in a sympathomimetic toxidrome, so they are second line after benzodiazepines rather than the first choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Benzodiazepines are first line for agitation and the sympathomimetic features of synthetic cannabinoid toxicity, and a quiet low stimulus environment reduces escalation and the need for restraint. Most episodes settle within hours with supportive care and observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Beta blockade in a sympathomimetic state leaves alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen hypertension, and treating the number does not address the agitation driving it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Standard immunoassay panels do not detect synthetic cannabinoids, so a negative screen does not exclude intoxication, and discharging an agitated hypertensive patient two hours into an evolving toxidrome is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A regular antipsychotic and psychiatric referral presume a primary psychotic illness, whereas these symptoms are substance induced and typically resolve within hours to days without ongoing treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Ketamine associated uropathy is an under recognised consequence of regular recreational use and typically presents as severe urinary frequency, suprapubic pain and haematuria with repeatedly sterile cultures. Patients are commonly treated for recurrent urinary tract infection for months before the substance history is taken. The damage is dose and duration related and ranges from inflammatory cystitis through to a small contracted bladder, ureteric stricture and hydronephrosis. Cessation is the central intervention and can reverse early disease, whereas continued use leads to irreversible structural damage that may require reconstruction.
key_points: Sterile pyuria or haematuria with severe frequency should prompt a substance history
Cessation can reverse early changes; established contracture cannot be reversed
Assess the upper tracts, because ureteric stricture and hydronephrosis are recognised complications
Ketamine also causes hepatobiliary damage with biliary dilatation and abnormal liver enzymes
explanation.pearls: Ask about ketamine in any young person with recurrent culture negative cystitis: the average delay from symptom onset to correct diagnosis runs to many months of repeated antibiotic courses, and every month of continued use narrows the window in which the bladder changes are still reversible.

sources.label: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage

options.rationale: Three sterile cultures have already excluded bacterial infection, and further antibiotics expose her to adverse effects and resistance while the causative exposure continues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antimuscarinic therapy is used for overactive bladder but gives limited benefit in this condition and does nothing to stop the ongoing injury, so it risks masking progression while the exposure continues. (Source: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage)
source_refs: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage

options.rationale: Chronic ketamine use causes an ulcerative cystitis with severe frequency, pain and haematuria and sterile urine, and stopping the drug is the only intervention that halts progression to irreversible bladder contracture and upper tract damage. Urology assessment with cystoscopy and upper tract imaging is needed because the damage can extend to ureteric stricture and hydronephrosis. (Source: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage)
source_refs: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage

options.rationale: A sexually transmitted cause is a reasonable thought in a young woman with urinary symptoms, but her screen is already negative and this does not explain two years of symptoms with sterile urine and haematuria. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Microscopic haematuria with persistent pain is never attributable to a functional disorder without investigation, and a year of continued use can produce a contracted bladder requiring reconstructive surgery. (Source: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage)
source_refs: NSW Health: Ketamine related bladder damage

explanation.summary: Distinguishing substance induced psychosis from a primary psychotic illness precipitated or unmasked by substance use is done through the course of symptoms during verified abstinence rather than at the first presentation. Methamphetamine induced psychosis characteristically resolves within days to a few weeks of stopping, whereas symptoms that persist well beyond that period, particularly when negative symptoms such as blunted affect and social withdrawal emerge, indicate a primary illness. The distinction matters because it determines whether antipsychotic treatment is short term or ongoing, and whether the person is offered the full early psychosis intervention package. A substantial proportion of people with methamphetamine associated psychosis go on to receive a diagnosis of schizophrenia.
key_points: Resolution within days to weeks of abstinence supports a substance induced disorder
Emerging negative symptoms favour a primary psychotic illness
Verified abstinence, ideally with supervised testing, is what makes the distinction interpretable
Continued substance use treatment remains essential regardless of which diagnosis applies
explanation.pearls: Do not let the diagnostic uncertainty delay early psychosis care: the first two to five years carry the greatest risk of disengagement and relapse, and a young man who is given ongoing antipsychotic treatment without vocational, family and relapse prevention support has had only part of the intervention that changes his trajectory.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Withdrawing treatment from a man with active delusions and hallucinations would worsen his illness, and the persistence of symptoms through abstinence is precisely the evidence that the substance is no longer the driver. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Waiting without altering the formulation delays access to family intervention, vocational support and relapse prevention that early psychosis services provide, and the diagnostic question has already been answered by eight weeks of abstinence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Hair testing would extend the detection window but eight weeks of supervised random negative samples in a residential setting already provides strong evidence of abstinence, and the result would not change the need for continued treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Substance induced psychotic disorder resolves within days to weeks of abstinence, so psychotic symptoms persisting through eight weeks of verified abstinence, with emerging negative symptoms, indicate a primary psychotic illness that requires ongoing antipsychotic treatment and the full package of early psychosis care. Supervised negative screens make continued covert use an unlikely explanation. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated when there are focal neurological signs, atypical features or an unusual age at onset, and his examination and course are typical of a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics reduce relapse in patients whose illness course is driven by non-adherence, and this man's history of three relapses after stopping oral medication is a clear indication. The safety principle that governs initiation is that a depot cannot be withdrawn once given: the drug continues to be released for weeks to months whatever adverse effect emerges. For this reason a patient who has never taken the chosen agent is first given the oral form to establish tolerability. Baseline metabolic and cardiac assessment and ongoing monitoring accompany treatment but do not substitute for the oral trial.
key_points: A depot cannot be removed, so tolerability must be established with the oral form first
Recurrent relapse related to non-adherence is the strongest indication for a long-acting injectable
Routine prophylactic anticholinergics are not recommended
Compulsory treatment provisions are irrelevant when the patient consents
explanation.pearls: Remember that a depot continues to release drug long after the last injection, so if a patient develops neuroleptic malignant syndrome on a long-acting injectable, the episode can run for weeks rather than the days seen with oral agents, and supportive care must be planned on that timescale.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: A period of observation detects an immediate reaction but not the subacute adverse effects that emerge over days, and once a depot is injected the drug continues to be released for weeks regardless of what develops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Routine anticholinergic prophylaxis is not recommended because it adds cognitive and peripheral adverse effects to a majority who will not develop extrapyramidal symptoms, and it is given when those symptoms actually appear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Cardiac monitoring is part of ongoing care but does not address the question of whether he tolerates this particular molecule, and it comes after the irreversible step has already been taken. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

He is consenting to treatment, so compulsory provisions are neither necessary nor lawful, and a legal order is not a substitute for establishing that the drug is tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A trial of the oral preparation establishes tolerability and screens for idiosyncratic reactions such as dystonia or a hypersensitivity response before committing the patient to a depot that cannot be removed once injected. This is standard practice whenever a patient has never been exposed to the chosen agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Bipolar depression is treated differently from unipolar depression because antidepressants carry a risk of switching the patient into mania or a mixed state and may accelerate cycling. Australian guidance therefore favours agents with evidence in bipolar depression specifically, of which quetiapine has the strongest monotherapy data, with lurasidone and lithium as alternatives and lamotrigine useful for prophylaxis of depressive episodes. If an antidepressant is used at all it is given alongside adequate mood stabilisation rather than as monotherapy. This woman's two previous manic admissions and eighteen months without prophylaxis make a treatment that covers both the current episode and future relapse the logical choice.
key_points: Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar depression because of switch and cycling risk
Quetiapine has the best evidence as monotherapy for the depressive phase
Dual acting antidepressants carry the highest switch rate
Always ask about a history of mania before prescribing an antidepressant for depression
explanation.pearls: Screen for a mixed state before prescribing: agitation, irritability and racing thoughts occurring within a depressive episode change the treatment entirely and are the presentation in which an antidepressant does the most harm.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Quetiapine has the strongest evidence as monotherapy for bipolar depression and treats the depressive episode without the risk of destabilising the illness that accompanies unopposed antidepressant use. It also provides prophylaxis against future mood episodes in someone with two previous manic episodes. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: An antidepressant given without a mood stabiliser in a patient with a history of mania risks a switch into mania or a mixed state, and monotherapy with a serotonergic antidepressant is specifically discouraged in bipolar depression. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Dual acting antidepressants carry a higher rate of switching into mania than other classes, so venlafaxine is the least suitable antidepressant choice in a patient with previous manic episodes. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines may provide short term relief of distress or insomnia but have no antidepressant efficacy and no prophylactic effect, and regular use risks dependence in a chronic relapsing illness. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy is a valuable component of care and should be offered, but for a moderate depressive episode in established bipolar disorder with prior admissions it is not sufficient alone. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Means restriction is the intervention with the best evidence for preventing suicide deaths at both the individual and population level. Suicidal crises are frequently brief and impulsive, and the lethality of the method available determines whether a crisis becomes a death, which is why firearm access matters so much in rural Australia. Asking directly about access to means is therefore a required part of every risk assessment, and negotiating removal to a licensed third party is more effective than relying on secure storage controlled by the person at risk. Treating the underlying depression and hazardous alcohol use, and arranging follow up, complete the plan but do not replace this step.
key_points: Ask every person with suicidal thoughts specifically about firearms, medication stockpiles and other means
Removal to a licensed third party is preferred to storage that the person at risk can still access
No harm contracts are ineffective and are not recommended
Hazardous alcohol use is both a risk factor and a modifiable treatment target
explanation.pearls: Rural men in Australia have markedly higher suicide rates than their urban counterparts, and firearm access is a large part of that difference; involving the wife in the conversation about where the guns will go turns an abstract safety plan into an arrangement that actually happens.

options.rationale: Pharmacological treatment of underlying depression is appropriate and should be considered, but it takes weeks to work and does not address the immediate lethality of the method available to him. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention resources)

Restricting access to a highly lethal method is the intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing suicide deaths, because suicidal crises are often short lived and the case fatality of firearms is far higher than other methods. Removal to a licensed third party is more effective than relying on the existing locked storage to which he alone has the key. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention resources)

No harm contracts have no evidence of effectiveness, provide false reassurance to the clinician and can damage the therapeutic relationship if the person feels unable to disclose worsening thoughts. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention resources)

Psychological therapy is an important part of the plan, but waiting lists in rural areas are long and therapy does not alter the immediate availability of a highly lethal method. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention resources)

He has no plan, no intent and is engaging voluntarily with good support, so compulsory admission is neither justified nor lawful, and it risks disengaging a man who has come forward willingly. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention resources)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics produce only modest benefit for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia and carry a significant increase in stroke and all cause mortality, along with sedation, parkinsonism and falls. They are therefore used only after reversible contributors such as pain, infection, constipation and environmental triggers have been addressed, and only when there is risk of harm or severe distress. When they are used, the duration is deliberately limited, with review and attempted withdrawal by about twelve weeks. Reduction should be gradual rather than abrupt, with monitoring for recurrence and a documented plan if symptoms return.
key_points: Exclude pain, infection, constipation and environmental triggers before prescribing
Review with a view to withdrawal by about twelve weeks
Most residents successfully discontinue without recurrence of the behaviour
Anticholinergics to treat drug induced parkinsonism worsen cognition and should be avoided
explanation.pearls: Emerging cogwheel rigidity and afternoon drowsiness in an older person on an antipsychotic are the signal to reduce rather than to add a second drug; falls in this group carry a high risk of hip fracture and the medication is a reversible contributor.

sources.label: RANZCP: Antipsychotic medications as a treatment of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.rationale: Indefinite continuation is the commonest error in this setting and exposes her to a cumulative and largely avoidable risk of stroke and death, particularly once the behaviour has resolved and a non-pharmacological plan is working. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Substituting a different antipsychotic maintains the class risks of sedation, falls and cerebrovascular events when the indication for any antipsychotic has passed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics for behavioural symptoms in dementia should be reviewed with a view to withdrawal by around twelve weeks, because benefit is modest and the risks of stroke, falls, parkinsonism and death accumulate with continued use. Her emerging rigidity, sedation and falls are evidence that harm is already outweighing benefit now that the target behaviour has settled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticholinergic medication worsens cognition and delirium risk in dementia and treats an adverse effect that would disappear if the causative drug were withdrawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Withdrawal is correct but abrupt cessation risks cholinergic rebound and recurrence of the behaviour, so a staged reduction with monitoring and a clear plan if symptoms return is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Opioid agonist treatment is continued throughout pregnancy because it is protective: it stabilises the maternal opioid level, keeps women engaged with antenatal care, and prevents the overdose, infection and fetal loss associated with relapse to illicit use. Neonatal abstinence syndrome occurs in a substantial proportion of exposed infants but is anticipated, monitored and treated, and its severity does not track reliably with maternal dose. Dose requirements often rise rather than fall through the third trimester because of increased volume of distribution and metabolism. Breastfeeding is encouraged on either agent and reduces the severity of neonatal withdrawal.
key_points: Relapse risk, not teratogenicity, is the dominant danger to the pregnancy
Neonatal abstinence syndrome severity does not correlate reliably with maternal dose
Do not switch a woman who is stable on one agonist to the other
Dose requirements commonly increase in the third trimester
explanation.pearls: Plan the postnatal dose explicitly: the physiological changes of pregnancy reverse within days of birth, so a woman whose dose was increased in the third trimester can become over sedated postpartum unless the dose is reviewed in the first week.

sources.label: National guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.rationale: Medically supervised withdrawal in pregnancy is associated with high rates of relapse, and relapse is associated with overdose, blood borne virus transmission, poor antenatal attendance and stillbirth.
